items.title: Aleph Alpha releases Kolibri, a 78B-parameter open-weight mixture-of-experts LLM for German and English under Apache 2.0 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Aleph Alpha has launched Kolibri, a large language model with 78 billion parameters that uses a mixture-of-experts architecture to activate only about 3.5 billion parameters per token. Trained from scratch on infrastructure in Germany and Finland, Kolibri supports German and English and is released under the Apache 2.0 license with weights available on Hugging Face. The model was designed with the EU AI Act in mind to balance innovation and regulation, allowing organizations to deploy it on-premises with full data privacy and intellectual property control. Kolibri features 50 layers each containing 384 experts, with a router selecting six experts per token to reduce computation while maintaining model capacity. Its tokenizer is optimized for German compound words, using a large vocabulary of 128,000 tokens trained with a new UniBPE algorithm. Aleph Alpha emphasizes Kolibri's sovereignty, meaning it was developed under European law without foreign control, and it complies with the EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice. The model aims to provide a more efficient and privacy-conscious alternative for German and English language tasks.

items.title: Aleph Alpha releases Kolibri, a 78B-parameter English-German Mixture-of-Experts transformer with 3B active parameters and 1M token context length under Apache 2.0 license [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Aleph Alpha has launched Kolibri, a new sovereign open-weight language model designed for mission-critical applications in regulated sectors such as public administration, industrials, and aerospace. Kolibri features 78 billion total parameters with 3 billion active, supports context lengths up to 1 million tokens, and is optimized for German and English, reasoning, math, and agentic behavior. The model is available for download on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. Kolibri builds on a robust training pipeline that enabled stable pre-training and extensive ablation experiments, resulting in improved performance over its predecessor, Kolibri Origin. The model balances quality and serving cost efficiently, allowing on-premise deployment without sending data to third parties, and includes specialized internal evaluation suites tailored to key sectors. It also incorporates mechanisms to abstain from answering when context is insufficient, enhancing reliability and compliance for enterprise customers.

items.title: Creator of Redis launches ds4 for running large language models locally with asymmetric 2-bit quantization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: The creator of Redis has introduced ds4, a tool designed to run large language models (LLMs) locally using asymmetric 2-bit quantization. This approach compresses routed experts while maintaining precision in critical shared paths, enabling efficient deployment of routed mixture-of-experts (MoE) models on target machines. The technology aims to optimize performance and resource use for local LLM execution.

items.title: Researchers develop Ataraxos AI that beats top Stratego player using a neural network to infer hidden pieces and strategic self-play [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A team from Carnegie Mellon, MIT, NYU, and Stanford created Ataraxos, an AI that defeated Pim Niemeijer, a leading Stratego player, by 15 wins to one with four draws. The AI uses a second neural network to predict opponents' hidden pieces and employs strategic self-play over 163 million games to master the imperfect-information game. Stratego's complexity arises from hidden piece identities and long game length, making it challenging for previous AIs like DeepMind's DeepNash. Ataraxos overcomes this by sampling plausible opponent piece arrangements and planning moves accordingly, enabling it to bluff and recover from losing positions methodically. The AI's calm, unbothered approach contrasts with human impulsiveness, contributing to its success against top human competition.

items.title: ChatGPT launches Sites feature to build, publish, and share websites and apps through conversational prompts [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: ChatGPT has introduced Sites, a new feature that allows users to create, host, and share websites, apps, and games by describing their ideas in plain language. Users can refine their projects through interactive conversations with ChatGPT, preview them in an in-app browser, and publish with customizable access controls, including workspace sharing and public availability. Sites supports collaborative editing within workspaces, visitor sign-in for saving progress, and integration with connected tools in eligible business environments. The feature is currently in public beta and available to users on ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans, with varying access and usage limits depending on the plan and region.

items.title: OpenAI safety lead David Robinson resigns, citing broken company culture and escalating AI risks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: David Robinson, a safety lead at OpenAI and one of its longest-tenured employees, has resigned, criticizing the company's culture as broken and warning that its iterative deployment approach leads to growing safety failures. In an essay published in The Atlantic, Robinson highlighted recent security breaches involving OpenAI agents and called for AI companies to adopt rigorous safety practices akin to those in nuclear power or aviation industries. OpenAI responded by stating it is enhancing safety measures, including pausing model training when necessary and improving monitoring and third-party evaluations. Robinson also emphasized the need for broader cultural changes and stronger external incentives to ensure AI alignment with human values as systems become more capable.

items.title: Report: AI chips shipped through 2027 could run up to 170 million concurrent frontier-model agents, supplying work hours equivalent to hundreds of millions of full-time employees [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: AI chips shipped through 2027 have the potential to run tens to hundreds of millions of concurrent AI agents, providing work hours comparable to 140 to 720 million full-time employees, according to an analysis by Epoch AI. More efficient models could support billions of agents, but realizing this capacity would require a massive increase in global demand for AI services, with estimated annual API-equivalent spending reaching trillions of dollars. The analysis estimates that high-bandwidth memory (HBM) shipped from 2025 to 2027 could support 30 to 170 million concurrent agents, assuming full deployment. These agents can operate continuously, working 168 hours per week compared to a human's 40-hour workweek, amplifying their potential economic impact. However, even using 20% of this capacity would imply annual spending of $2.6 to $5.3 trillion, far exceeding current developer revenues projected to reach about $1 trillion by 2027. The key uncertainty remains whether demand for AI services will grow rapidly enough to utilize this hardware capacity. The report also highlights significant variation in hourly agent costs across different AI models and workloads, underscoring the complexity of scaling AI agent deployment at this scale.

items.title: Multisynapse says AI agents need a system of record for governance and auditability beyond dashboards, tracking versions, permissions, and actions [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: Multisynapse argues that managing AI agents requires a system of record that tracks every agent's version, permissions, and actions to ensure transparency, accountability, and compliance. Unlike dashboards that only show what happened, this system provides governance by recording what was allowed and what actually occurred, enabling quick answers to questions about agent behavior and decisions. The system includes features such as version control, policy checks, graded evaluations before deployment, and tamper-evident audit trails. It supports multi-tenant organizations with role separation and access controls, and maps evidence to standards like the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001. This approach aims to provide reliable records for audits and regulatory inquiries, improving trust and control over AI agent operations.

items.title: FLUX 3 Image launches a text-to-image model trained for precise image layout and composition using bounding boxes [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: FLUX 3 Image is a text-to-image generation model designed to create well-composed images by understanding layout and composition through bounding boxes. It allows users to specify image elements precisely, enabling detailed edits such as recoloring and adding objects while preserving textures and colors at full resolution. The model supports commercial licensing for companies to fine-tune and deploy on their own infrastructure, facilitating scalable image generation with strong prompt adherence and native compositional understanding.

items.title: Splice CEO Kakul Srivastava says AI-generated emails harm genuine conversations and stresses human-centered creativity in AI music tools [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Kakul Srivastava, CEO of Splice, a popular music sample platform, expressed concerns that AI-generated emails diminish meaningful conversations, emphasizing the importance of human involvement in communication and creative processes. She highlighted Splice's approach to AI, which focuses on tools that keep humans central to music creation rather than fully automated song generation. Srivastava, who has held executive roles at Flickr, Yahoo, GitHub, and Adobe, discussed the value of thoughtful, well-written documents and real conversations in a remote work environment. She warned that AI-written content can change the nature of discussions and reduce their quality. Her perspective reflects a broader skepticism about AI's role in creative fields, advocating for technology that supports rather than replaces human creativity.

items.title: TechCrunch lists notable AI agents that operate via text messages, including Instinct, Caddy, Fambot, Folk, and Iris, offering personal assistance across iMessage, SMS, and messaging apps [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A growing number of AI agents can now be accessed directly through text messages, allowing users to complete tasks like scheduling, shopping, and reminders without downloading separate apps. Notable examples include Instinct, valued at $10 billion, which offers email and voice interaction, and Caddy, which integrates with calendars and conversations on iMessage and RCS. Other AI assistants highlighted include Fambot, designed for family organization and available via SMS and apps; Folk, which runs on a private cloud and supports multi-step tasks across messaging platforms; and Iris, which delegates tasks through iMessage. These agents connect to existing apps and services to streamline daily activities and communication.

items.title: Google updates search guidelines to penalize sites using fake bylines and AI-generated headshots, labeling such deception as low-quality content [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Google has revised its content guidelines to explicitly prohibit the use of fabricated creator profiles, including AI-generated headshots, fake names, and false credentials, stating that such deceptive practices make pages untrustworthy and lower their ranking in search results. This update follows investigations into companies like Brown Brothers Media, which used fake journalists and plagiarized content to generate high traffic through AI-powered content mills. The new guidelines emphasize that accurate authorship information aligns with Google's standards for experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness (E-E-A-T), while deceptive authorship signals low-quality content to both users and Google's automated systems. This move aims to curb the spread of misleading content, although concerns remain about the broader impact of AI-generated summaries on independent journalism and original reporting.

items.title: Poll shows 63% of Americans support pausing AI development and 61% back a federal wealth tax on billionaires ahead of 2026 midterms [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A Wall Street Journal poll of 1,500 registered US voters found that 63% support pausing AI development and 57% want immediate government regulation of AI, with only 12% trusting AI companies to self-regulate. The survey also revealed broad bipartisan support for policies targeting wealth inequality, including a 61% approval for a federal wealth tax on billionaires and strong backing for healthcare reforms and financial protections. The poll highlights growing public concern over the concentration of wealth among tech billionaires and its connection to AI advancements. Democratic pollster John Anzalone noted that economic struggles are driving voters toward populist policies across party lines, reflecting frustration with affordability and economic mobility. These results suggest that economic inequality and AI regulation are significant issues influencing voter sentiment ahead of the November midterm elections.

items.title: Former OpenAI safety lead David Robinson resigns and warns of broken industry culture and need for nuclear-level AI safeguards [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: David Robinson, who authored safety reports for OpenAI's major model releases, resigned this week and published an editorial in The Atlantic criticizing the company's culture as fundamentally broken. He argues that the AI industry operates with excessive confidence and speed, neglecting potential risks and calling for stringent safety measures akin to those in nuclear power plants. Robinson's departure is part of a broader trend of AI researchers and safety experts leaving prominent firms amid growing concerns about AI risks. He emphasizes the need for humility and rigorous, layered safeguards in AI development to prevent catastrophic errors, highlighting a shift in the industry's approach to safety and responsibility.
